### Abstract

Each year in the United States, up to 900,000 individuals will suffer from acute pulmonary embolism, resulting in an estimated 200,000 to 300,000 hospital admissions. Despite decades of research on the topic, the diagnosis remains elusive in many situations and the fatality rate remains significant. This issue presents a review of the current evidence guiding the emergency medicine approach to the diagnosis and treatment of pulmonary embolism. Key to this approach is the concept of risk stratification: using factors from the history and physical examination, plus ancillary tests, to guide clinical decision making. The pathophysiology of pulmonary embolism and decision-support tools are reviewed, and emergency department management strategies are described.

### Case Presentations

*A 49-year-old male construction worker presents to the ED reporting a brief loss of consciousness 30 minutes prior to arrival while climbing through a crawlspace at work. He reports a prodrome of feeling short of breath, lightheaded, and dizzy, with associated midsternal chest pain. Family members at the bedside report that he was complaining of generalized weakness with mild shortness of breath at rest and on exertion for the past 3 to 4 days. His past medical history is significant for rectal cancer treated with resection, a traumatic fracture of L3, and deep vein thrombosis 9 months ago, after which he completed a 6-month course of warfarin. The patient denies use of tobacco, alcohol consumption, or use of illicit drugs. There is no family history of any medical problems. His vital signs upon arrival are: temperature, 36°C; blood pressure, 104/79 mm Hg; heart rate, 106 beats per minute; respiratory rate, 20 breaths per minute; and oxygen saturation, 95% on room air. He is in no distress, is sitting upright on the stretcher, and is speaking in full sentences. Aside from a regular tachycardia, his exam is normal. Initial ECG shows a sinus tachycardia at 106 beats per minute, rightward axis deviation, ST-segment depressions throughout, and deep T-wave inversions in the anterolateral leads. Laboratory analysis, including cardiac markers, electrolytes, CBC, and renal function are remarkable only for a platelet count of 115,000 x 109/L. Initial cardiac markers and electrolytes are normal. You put acute coronary syndromes on the top of your differential and admit the patient to the observation unit, but you wonder if there is anything else that should be done while waiting for the second troponin...*

*A short time later, a 58-year-old male with a history of hypertension presents to the ED with leg pain. He woke up 2 days prior with pain and discoloration of his right leg, which has progressively worsened. Although not initially reported in the chief complaint, upon review of systems, the patient reports that he has been dizzy and short of breath for the past couple of days. He denies chest pain, diaphoresis, or syncope. The patient further denies history of coagulopathy or prior blood clots. On exam, he is well-appearing and in no distress. He is afebrile, is tachycardic at 117 beats per minute, is breathing at a rate of 16 breaths per minute, and has a blood pressure of 155/93 mm Hg. His oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. The physical exam is remarkable only for the right lower extremity. The entire right leg is diffusely tender, with edema, erythema, and plethora. Laboratory results are unremarkable; ECG is normal sinus rhythm at a rate of 98 beats per minute with left axis deviation and no ST-segment abnormalities.*

### Introduction

Each year in the United States, it is estimated that between 600,000 and 900,000 individuals suffer from acute pulmonary embolism (PE), accounting for an estimated 200,000 to 300,000 hospital admissions.1-4 In the United States, as many as 100,000 deaths are estimated to be caused by venous thromboembolism each year. Furthermore, numerous studies have found that approximately 1% of all patients admitted to hospitals die of acute PE, and an estimated 10% of all hospital deaths are PE related.5-7 If left untreated, PE can be rapidly fatal.2,8,9

Improvements in detection and treatment of deep vein thromboses, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis protocols, and improvements in the sensitivity and specificity of diagnostic tests have resulted in a substantially decreased overall mortality from PE in the past decade.3,10 Nonetheless, despite these advancements, PE still remains a fatal pathology, with a mortality rate of up to 10% of all patients diagnosed with an acute PE in the first 1 to 3 months following diagnosis.11,12 While the mortality of PE is well publicized, the morbidity associated with undiagnosed PE is not, and it can be very disabling, leading to both pulmonary hypertension and postthrombotic syndrome.4,13-15 This issue of *Emergency Medicine Practice* presents a review of the current evidence guiding the emergency medicine approach to the diagnosis and treatment of PE.

### Critical Appraisal Of The Literature

An extensive literature search was performed using the PubMed database, Ovid MEDLINE®, and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. Searches were limited to the English language. Search terms included, but were not limited to the following: *pulmonary embolism, venous thromboembolism, emergency department, treatment, risk stratification, prevention, deep vein thrombosis, and cancer.* Search results for *pulmonary embolism* returned 13,305 articles. The search was further limited to include only clinical trials, meta-analyses, practice guidelines, randomized controlled trials, and reviews, returning 3378 publications. The breadth of the available literature is extensive; thus, clinical trials and guidelines were only reviewed if published within the last decade. The National Guideline Clearinghouse ([www.guidelines.gov](http://www.guidelines.gov)) and the American College of Emergency Physicians (ACEP) Clinical Policies were referenced for PE management, risk stratification, and prevention guidelines and policies. The bibliographies of these guidelines were also reviewed. A total of 98 references were used in the preparation of this article.

As noted earlier, the number of publications on the topic of PE is extensive, with articles dating back over a century and multiplying exponentially in the last decade. There has been a great expansion in the literature around PE in the last 10 to 20 years. Studies typically focus on either the diagnosis or the treatment of PE, but there are several limitations in the literature regarding both of these types of studies. Diagnostic studies are typically limited by the relatively low prevalence of PE, so maintaining high sensitivity with narrow confidence intervals often requires a multicenter trial in order to enroll enough patients. Nonetheless, several recent meta-analyses have added validity to the findings of smaller studies. An additional limitation for studies regarding the diagnosis of PE is the variability in the definition of a “true negative.” Studies vary widely regarding which “gold standard” (if any) is used to assess if the results of the diagnostic study in question are accurate. “Gold standard” tests vary from clinical follow-up to pulmonary angiography. Regarding treatment studies, the primary limitation is the lack of well-controlled studies in critically ill patients, where poor outcomes are most likely. The challenge of performing informed consent in this group is an important limitation of many studies aiming to evaluate treatment in the critically ill patient with PE. Consequently, studies evaluating the effectiveness of both medical and interventional treatments for those who are the most unstable are often small retrospective studies or large database reviews where the patient populations included in the various studies are difficult to compare or specifics regarding the patients are not available.

### Risk Management Pitfalls For Pulmonary Embolism

1. **“PE wasn’t a part of this patient’s differential.”**

   Consider PE in patients with the most-common complaints (chest pain and shortness of breath), but also with less-common complaints such as syncope, dizziness, or anxiety. PE can present with a multitude of complaints, and it is essential to keep a low threshold when deciding to include it in the differential.
2. **“This patient was in shock. I thought he was septic.”**

   Always consider massive PE in the differential of undifferentiated atraumatic shock.
3. **“Her PERC score was negative, so I didn’t think I had to order any tests.”**

   Application of the PERC rule must be confined to a patient population already deemed by the practitioner as low risk. A negative PERC score does not have a negative predictive value high enough to be utilized in any other risk category.
4. **“The D-dimer at triage was negative, so I didn’t think I had to worry about PE.”**

   Reliance on D-dimer tests other than the quantitative turbidimetric or ELISA assays is inappropriate. Interrater reliability with the qualitative assays used in many point-of-care assays is inadequate, and the sensitivity of this test is not adequate, particularly in the undifferentiated patient.
5. **“I knew the quantitative D-dimer test is much better than the bedside assays. Since it was negative, I stopped the work-up there.”**

   As with the PERC rule, interpretation of a negative D-dimer assay must be done in the context of the clinician’s pretest probability for disease. Current evidence shows that only in patients considered to have a low clinical risk for PE can a negative quantitative D-dimer safely exclude PE.
6. **“The CTPA was negative, so I discharged the patient.”**

   As with prior tests mentioned, a negative CTPA (or indeterminate V/Q scan) does not rule out the possibility of PE in a patient considered high risk for emboli. The clinician must interpret the negative results in the context of pretest probability of disease.
7. **“I started the heparin, and his vitals were fine, so I admitted him to the floor.”**

   A significant percentage of initially stable patients with pulmonary emboli will deteriorate during their hospital course, requiring escalation of therapy. Evaluation of the patient’s potential for deterioration will aid the clinician in admitting the patient to the correct setting.
8. **“I held the heparin pending the results of his diagnostic tests. I knew he was really tachycardic,**

   **but I haven’t confirmed the diagnosis yet.”**

   In a patient with a high clinical suspicion for disease and signs of hemodynamic instability, initiate anticoagulation therapy immediately. Delayed treatment is associated with increased mortality in these patients.
9. **“I started the patient on 120 mg of enoxaparin. She was dialyzed yesterday.”**

   Failure to evaluate for contraindications to specific treatment options can cause significant complications. Patients with renal compromise should be treated with unfractionated heparin. As with all therapeutics, the emergency clinician must have a good understanding of both the indications and contraindications for any therapy initiated.
10. **“I know she was stable, but I thought she would benefit from thrombolytics.”**

    Although controversy exists regarding the use of thrombolytic therapy in patients with PE, they are not recommended in stable patients, since the risks outweigh the benefits.

# Reproducibility of CT Signs of Right Ventricular Dysfunction in Acute Pulmonary Embolism

Authors: [Doo Kyoung Kang](#con1), [Luis Ramos-Duran](#con2), [U. Joseph Schoepf](#con3), [Andrew M. Armstrong](#con4), [Joseph A. Abro](#con5), [James G. Ravenel](#con6), and [Christian Thilo](#con7)[Author Info & Affiliations](#tab-contributors)

[Volume 194, Issue 6](/toc/ajr/194/6)

[4,35753](# "Metrics")

## Abstract

**OBJECTIVE.** The purpose of our study was to determine the interobserver reproducibility of CT findings of right ventricular (RV) dysfunction in pulmonary embolism (PE).

**MATERIALS AND METHODS.** Two experienced observers independently and retrospectively evaluated pulmonary CT angiography (CTA) studies of 50 patients with acute PE for the following signs: bowing of the interventricular septum, inferior vena cava (IVC) contrast medium reflux, RV diameter (RVD)/left ventricular diameter (LVD) ratio on axial sections and four-chamber (4-CH) views, and RV volume (RVV)/left ventricular volume (LVV) ratio. Analysis used kappa statistics, Spearman's rank correlation, and Bland-Altman statistics.

**RESULTS.** The two observers had fair to moderate agreement (κ = 0.32–0.44) for septal bowing and moderate to good agreement (κ = 0.57–0.68) for diagnosing IVC reflux. The Spearman's rank correlation coefficients for RVDaxial/LVDaxial ratio and RVD4-CH/LVD4-CH ratio between the two observers were 0.88 (*p* < 0.001) and 0.85 (*p* < 0.001), respectively. On Bland-Altman analysis, the mean differences for RVDaxial/LVDaxial ratio and RVD4-CH/LVD4-CH ratio were 0.014 (± 0.195) and 0.001 (± 0.242), respectively. The correlation coefficient for RVV/LVV ratio was 0.93 (*p* < 0.001), and the mean difference was 0.033 (± 0.229).

**CONCLUSION.** Considerable differences exist in the interobserver reproducibility of CT findings of RV dysfunction on pulmonary CTA in patients with acute PE. Cardiac chamber measurements are more reproducible than septal bowing and IVC reflux. Volumetric determination of the RVV/LVV ratio is the least user dependent and most reproducible.

## Introduction

Acute pulmonary embolism (PE) is a common disease with a 3-month mortality rate of up to 17.4% [[1](#core-collateral-REF1)–[4](#core-collateral-REF4)]. Even if PE is properly treated with anticoagulation, the mortality rate in hemodynamically stable patients varies from 8.1% to 15.1% [[4](#core-collateral-REF4), [5](#core-collateral-REF5)]. Death is usually caused by acute right heart failure [[4](#core-collateral-REF4)–[9](#core-collateral-REF9)]. Acute PE increases the pressure of the pulmonary arterial system and right ventricle (RV) resulting in RV dysfunction, which may progress to right heart failure and circulatory collapse [[5](#core-collateral-REF5), [6](#core-collateral-REF6)]. Patients with RV dysfunction have a higher mortality rate than those without, even if they are initially hemodynamically stable [[6](#core-collateral-REF6), [7](#core-collateral-REF7)]. Thus, the presence of RV dysfunction is a marker for adverse clinical outcome in patients with acute PE [[6](#core-collateral-REF6)–[8](#core-collateral-REF8)]. Echocardiography is the most common first-line examination to diagnose the signs of RV dysfunction [[6](#core-collateral-REF6)–[9](#core-collateral-REF9)]. However, this test has limited off-hour availability at many institutions, and occasionally the RV may be difficult to image with the trans thoracic approach.

Contrast medium–enhanced pulmonary CT angiography (CTA) is increasingly used as the first-line imaging test in suspected PE and is available 24 hours a day at most institutions [[10](#core-collateral-REF10)–[14](#core-collateral-REF14)]. Pulmonary CTA not only allows direct visualization of emboli but provides information regarding the status of the right heart [[15](#core-collateral-REF15), [16](#core-collateral-REF16)]. In several studies, the ratio of the RV to left ventricle (LV) diameters on pulmonary CTA has been proposed as a sign for RV dysfunction [[17](#core-collateral-REF17)–[19](#core-collateral-REF19)]. Other signs have been described, including bowing of the interventricular septum and reflux of contrast medium into the inferior vena cava (IVC) [[20](#core-collateral-REF20), [21](#core-collateral-REF21)]. However, a variety of different methods for the quantitative assessment of RV dysfunction on pulmonary CTA have been proposed [[17](#core-collateral-REF17)–[24](#core-collateral-REF24)] and the literature shows variable results for the prognostic power of pulmonary CTA signs of RV dysfunction to predict adverse outcomes. This variability may in part be explained by the somewhat subjective nature of diagnosing RV dysfunction on pulmonary CTA because formal criteria for establishing these signs are not available. It is noteworthy that several prior publications on this topic [[20](#core-collateral-REF20), [25](#core-collateral-REF25)–[27](#core-collateral-REF27)] do not report interobserver reproducibility of the findings. Accordingly, the purpose of our study was to determine the interobserver reproducibility of pulmonary CTA findings previously described to indicate RV dysfunction with the goal of identifying the most robust, least observer dependent method.

## Materials and Methods

### Patients

Our human research committee approved the study design and waived the need for informed patient consent for this retrospective, HIPAA-compliant analysis. We retrospectively identified 52 consecutive patients hospitalized at our institution between October 2008 and August 2009 with acute PE diagnosed on pulmonary CTA. A total of 50 patients were eligible for the current study after two patients were excluded because of insufficient contrast enhancement of the ventricular chambers for reliably delineating the endocardial borders. The mean age of the subjects was 56 ± 15 years. Fifty-eight percent (*n* = 29) of patients were women and 42% (*n* = 21) were men. For indicating imaging work-up of suspected PE, our institution generally follows the recommendations as outlined by the Christopher Study Investigators [[28](#core-collateral-REF28)] and Piazza et al. [[29](#core-collateral-REF29)]. All patients included in this study had undergone a clinical assessment of the probability of pulmonary embolism, using the Wells scoring system [[30](#core-collateral-REF30)] by a medical attending physician. Our study population included 33 patients with high probability according to the Wells score and 17 patients with abnormal d-dimer test.

### Pulmonary CTA Acquisition

All patients had undergone non-ECG-gated pulmonary CTA on a 64-MDCT system (Somatom Sensation, Siemens Healthcare). Image acquisition parameters were 0.33 millisecond gantry rotation time, 32 × 0.6 mm collimation with *z*-flying focal spot technique, 120 kV, 160 mAseff, pitch of 1.2, and a reconstructed section thickness of 1 mm. Contrast medium enhancement was achieved with 100 mL of a nonionic iodinated contrast medium (iopromide, Ultravist 370, Bayer Healthcare) injected at 4 mL/s. Automated bolus triggering was used with a region of interest in the main pulmonary artery and a threshold of 100 HU for triggering data acquisition.

### Pulmonary CTA Interpretation

All pulmonary CTA studies were independently reviewed by two observers with 6 and 3 years of posttraining experience in cardiothoracic CT. Observers were blinded to the patients' clinical characteristics. Studies were reviewed electronically on a clinical workstation (Multi Modality Workplace, Siemens Healthcare). The window and level settings were individually adjusted for each patient study for optimized display of pulmonary emboli and the cardiac chambers. The initial clinical diagnosis of PE was confirmed in the presence of at least one filling defect in the pulmonary artery tree, including the subsegmental level [[11](#core-collateral-REF11)–[15](#core-collateral-REF15)]. The observers assessed the most central level of involvement of PE.

*Septal bowing—*Deviation of the interventricular septum was evaluated as follows: normal (convex toward the RV), flattened septum, and septal bowing (convex toward the LV) [[17](#core-collateral-REF17), [20](#core-collateral-REF20)].

*IVC reflux—*The severity of reflux of contrast medium into the IVC or hepatic veins was graded using axial images according to six categories according to a previously published scale [[21](#core-collateral-REF21)]: 1, no reflux into IVC; 2, trace of reflux into IVC only; 3, reflux into IVC but not hepatic veins; 4, reflux into IVC with opacification of proximal hepatic veins; 5, reflux into IVC with opacification of hepatic veins down to the midportion of the liver; and 6, reflux into IVC with opacification of distal hepatic veins.

Fig. 2A **—**CT signs of right ventricle (RV) dysfunction in 57-year-old woman with acute pulmonary embolism. Four-chamber view shows septal bowing (*arrow*), convex toward left ventricle (LV).

![](/cms/10.2214/AJR.09.3717/asset/images/06_09_3717_02b.jpeg)

Fig. 2B **—**CT signs of right ventricle (RV) dysfunction in 57-year-old woman with acute pulmonary embolism. CT image shows grade 5 reflux of contrast medium into inferior vena cava (*short arrow*) and proximal hepatic veins (*long arrows*).

Fig. 2C **—**CT signs of right ventricle (RV) dysfunction in 57-year-old woman with acute pulmonary embolism. CT images of measurements of maximal RV (**C**) and LV (**D**) diameters on transverse sections show axial RV diameter (RVD)/axial LV diameter (LVD) ratio of 1.3.

Fig. 2D **—**CT signs of right ventricle (RV) dysfunction in 57-year-old woman with acute pulmonary embolism. CT images of measurements of maximal RV (**C**) and LV (**D**) diameters on transverse sections show axial RV diameter (RVD)/axial LV diameter (LVD) ratio of 1.3.

Fig. 2E **—**CT signs of right ventricle (RV) dysfunction in 57-year-old woman with acute pulmonary embolism. CT images of measurements of maximal RV (**E**) and LV (**F**) diameters on four-chamber views show four-chamber RVD/four-chamber LVD ratio of 1.4.

![](/cms/10.2214/AJR.09.3717/asset/images/06_09_3717_02f.jpeg)

Fig. 2F **—**CT signs of right ventricle (RV) dysfunction in 57-year-old woman with acute pulmonary embolism. CT images of measurements of maximal RV (**E**) and LV (**F**) diameters on four-chamber views show four-chamber RVD/four-chamber LVD ratio of 1.4.

Fig. 2G **—**CT signs of right ventricle (RV) dysfunction in 57-year-old woman with acute pulmonary embolism. Semiautomated volumetry images of RV (pink) and LV (orange) displayed on transverse sections (**G**) and as coronal reformat (**H**) show RV volume/LV volume ratio of 2.57.

![](/cms/10.2214/AJR.09.3717/asset/images/06_09_3717_02h_cmyk.jpeg)

Fig. 2H **—**CT signs of right ventricle (RV) dysfunction in 57-year-old woman with acute pulmonary embolism. Semiautomated volumetry images of RV (pink) and LV (orange) displayed on transverse sections (**G**) and as coronal reformat (**H**) show RV volume/LV volume ratio of 2.57.

*RV diameter (RVD)/LV diameter (LVD) ratio—* The two observers identified the two axial sections that showed the maximal distance between the ventricular endocardium and the interventricular septum, perpendicular to the long axis of the heart [[22](#core-collateral-REF22), [23](#core-collateral-REF23)], for the RV and LV, respectively. RVDaxial and LVDaxial were subsequently measured and the RVDaxial / LVDaxial ratio was calculated. Next, observers independently reconstructed four-chamber views on the workstation using the approach illustrated in Figure [1A](#FIG1), [1B](#FIG2), [1C](#FIG3), [1D](#FIG4). The two observers then identified the two levels on the reconstructed four-chamber views that showed the maximal distance between the ventricular endocardium and the interventricular septum for the RV and LV, respectively. RVDfour-chamber (4-CH) and LVD4-CH were subsequently calculated.

*RVV/LVV ratio—*The volumetric analysis of both ventricles was performed by using the volume analysis application of the workstation (Volume Analysis Software, version VE31A, Siemens Healthcare). The endocardial contours were semi-automatically segmented from the valvular plane down to the apex of both ventricles. This involved manually outlining the endocardial contours on the transverse sections comprising the minimal and maximal expanse of the ventricle, which were then automatically propagated to the neighboring sections. The RVV/LVV ratio was subsequently calculated. The time needed for performing workstation volumetric measurements was recorded.

### Statistical Analysis

Interobserver reproducibility for determining the grade of IVC reflux and the position of the interventricular septum were calculated using unweighted kappa statistics. The kappa value for agreement was interpreted as follows: poor, < 0.20; fair, 0.21–0.40; moderate, 0.41–0.60; good, 0.61–0.80; and very good, 0.81–1.00 [[31](#core-collateral-REF31)]. For continuous variables, agreement between the two observers was assessed using Spearman's rank correlation and Bland-Altman analysis [[32](#core-collateral-REF32)]. We used MedCalc (version 10.4.8, MedCalc Software) for all statistical analyses.

## Results

The initial clinical diagnosis of acute PE, which had served as an inclusion criterion, was confirmed by both observers in all 50 patients. The most central level of involvement with PE was found in the main pulmonary arteries in 12 patients (24%) and at the segmental pulmonary arterial level in 24 (48%); 14 patients (28%) had PE isolated to the subsegmental level. Within 30 days of follow-up, one patient died and 10 patients suffered an adverse clinical event including six who required endotracheal intubation, five requiring thrombolysis, one requiring vasopressors, and one cardiopulmonary resuscitation. During 9 months of follow-up, four patients (8%) died.

### Septal Bowing

Observer 1 classified the position of the interventricular septum as normal in 48% (*n* = 24) of patients, as flattened in 34% (*n* = 17), and as showing septal bowing in 18% (*n* = 9). Observer 2 described a normal position of the interventricular septum in 60% (*n* = 30) of patients, flattened septum in 32% (*n* = 16), and septal bowing in 8% (*n* = 4). Overall interobserver reproducibility for describing the position of the ventricular septum was fair (κ = 0.32; 95% CI, 0.090–0.551). For differentiating normal versus abnormal (flattening or bowing) position of the septum, reproducibility was moderate (κ = 0.44; 95% CI, 0.220–0.685) ([Fig. 2A](#FIG5)).

### IVC Reflux

Observer 1 classified the grade of reflux of contrast medium into the IVC as grade 1 in 30% (*n* = 15) of patients, as grade 2 in 30% (*n* = 15), grade 3 in 18% (*n* = 9), grade 4 in 10% (*n* = 5), grade 5 in 4% (*n* = 2), and grade 6 in 8% (*n* = 4). Observer 2 described the grade of IVC reflux as grade 1 in 22% (*n* = 11) of patients, grade 2 in 42% (*n* = 21), grade 3 in 20% (*n* = 10), grade 4 in 8% (*n* = 4), and grade 5 in 8% (*n* = 4). The degree of contrast medium reflux was grouped into no reflux (grade 1), minimal (grade 2 to 3), and substantial (grade 4 to 6). We found moderate agreement between the two observers for differentiating these three categories (κ = 0.57; 95% CI, 0.365–0.770), which reached good agreement (κ = 0.68; 95% CI, 0.408–0.946) when we evaluated differentiation between substantial (grade 4 to 6) and nonsubstantial reflux (grade 1 to 3) ([Fig. 2B](#FIG6)).

### RVD/LVD Ratio

The mean RVD and LVD on axial sections (Figs. [2C](#FIG7) and [2D](#FIG8)) measured by observer 1 and observer 2 were 4.5 ± 0.9 cm and 4.1 ± 0.9 cm, and 4.5 ± 0.7 cm and 4.0 ± 0.8 cm, respectively ([Table 1](#TBL1)). The mean RVD and LVD on four-chamber views (Figs. [2E](#FIG9) and [2F](#FIG10)) were 4.4 ± 0.7 cm and 3.9 ± 0.8 cm, and 4.5 ± 0.6 cm and 3.9 ± 0.8 cm, respectively ([Table 1](#TBL1)). The mean differences in RVD between the values measured on axial sections and four-chamber views were 0.05 ± 0.44 cm for observer 1 and –0.06 ± 0.48 cm for observer 2. The mean differences in LVD between the values measured on axial sections and four-chamber views were 0.19 ± 0.33 cm for observer 1 and 0.09 ± 0.33 cm for observer 2. Spearman's rank correlation coefficients for measurements of RVDaxial, LVDaxial, and RVDaxial/LVDaxial ratio between the two observers were 0.88, 0.87, and 0.88 (*p* < 0.001 for all correlations), respectively. On Bland-Altman analysis of RVDaxial/LVDaxial ratio measurements, the means and SDs between the two observers were 0.014 and 0.195, respectively ([Fig. 3](#FIG13)). Spearman's rank correlation coefficients for measurements of RVD4-CH, LVD4-CH, and RVD4-CH/LVD4-CH ratio between the two observers were 0.83, 0.82, and 0.85 (*p* < 0.001 for all correlations), respectively. On Bland-Altman analysis of RVD4-CH/LVD4-CH ratio measurements, the means and SDs between the two observers were 0.001 and 0.242, respectively ([Fig. 4](#FIG14)).

### RVV/LVV Ratio

The mean RVV and LVV (Figs. [2G](#FIG11) and [2H](#FIG12)) measured by observer 1 and observer 2 were 130.5 ± 48.9 mL and 92.6 ± 42.2 mL, and 130.1 ± 47.9 mL and 90.4 ± 39.9 mL, respectively. The mean RVV/LVV ratios were 1.68 ± 1.06 for observer 1 and 1.71 ± 1.14 for observer 2, respectively. Spearman's rank correlation coefficients between the two observers were 0.95 for RVV, 0.97 for LVV, and 0.93 for RVV/LVV ratio (*p* < 0.001 for all correlations). On Bland-Altman analysis of RVV/LVV ratio measurements, the means and SD between the two observers were 0.033 and 0.229, respectively ([Fig. 5](#FIG15)). The time needed to perform the volumetric workstation measurements was 374 ± 90 seconds (range, 224–613 seconds) for observer 1 and 442 ± 131 seconds (range, 227–652 seconds) for observer 2.

## Discussion

The presence of RV dysfunction is a marker for adverse clinical outcome in patients with acute PE [[6](#core-collateral-REF6)–[8](#core-collateral-REF8)]. Several series have shown promising results in correlating pulmonary CTA signs of RV dysfunction with clinical outcomes [[19](#core-collateral-REF19)–[24](#core-collateral-REF24)]. A number of different quantitative methods have been described to assess the complex-shaped RV for signs of dysfunction in patients with acute PE [[20](#core-collateral-REF20)–[24](#core-collateral-REF24)]. Reported signs of RV dysfunction include flattening or leftward bowing of the interventricular septum, reflux of contrast medium into the IVC, and differences in heart chamber size with enlargement of the right heart [[33](#core-collateral-REF33)]. Although these signs are regularly visible on pulmonary CTA in patients with acute PE, uniform criteria for their evaluation have not been established, and there is no uniformly accepted standard for measuring the ventricles on pulmonary CTA or for determining RV dysfunction. The results of our study suggest that considerable interindividual differences exist in the reproducibility of CT signs of RV dysfunction, which may in part explain the variability in published results for predicting adverse outcomes based on findings at pulmonary CTA [[25](#core-collateral-REF25)]. If these signs are used in clinical practice to make patient management decisions, practitioners should be aware of the variable degree of subjectivity and reproducibility associated with these observations.

![](/cms/10.2214/AJR.09.3717/asset/images/06_09_3717_03.jpeg)

Fig. 3 **—**Chart shows Bland-Altman analysis of axial right ventricle diameter (RVDaxial)/axial left ventricle diameter (LVDaxial) ratio measured by two observers.

![](/cms/10.2214/AJR.09.3717/asset/images/06_09_3717_04.jpeg)

Fig. 4 **—**Chart shows Bland-Altman analysis of four-chamber right ventricle diameter (RVD4-CH)/four-chamber left ventricle diameter (LVD4-CH) ratio measured by two observers.

![](/cms/10.2214/AJR.09.3717/asset/images/06_09_3717_05.jpeg)

Fig. 5 **—**Chart shows Bland-Altman analysis of right ventricle volume (RVV)/left ventricle volume (LVV) ratio measured by two observers.

### Septal Bowing

The interventricular septum, which normally bows toward the RV, may shift toward the LV related to increased right heart pressure with severe pulmonary arterial obstruction [[16](#core-collateral-REF16)]. Septal bowing is not specific for acute PE and can be found in numerous disorders resulting in increased pulmonary artery pressure. In patients with acute PE, Araoz et al. [[19](#core-collateral-REF19)] and Collomb et al. [[20](#core-collateral-REF20)] reported that ventricular septal bowing strongly predicted admission to the ICU. On the other hand, Araoz et al. [[19](#core-collateral-REF19)] and Van der Meer et al. [[26](#core-collateral-REF26)] did not find this sign to be predictive of death from acute PE. In our study, the rate of detection of septal bowing was lower (18% for observer 1, 8% for observer 2) than the 23% reported by Araoz et al. [[19](#core-collateral-REF19)] or the 21% in the Van der Meer cohort [[26](#core-collateral-REF26)] and showed a high degree of interobserver variability (κ = 0.32–0.44). These findings correspond to the only fair reproducibility (κ = 0.54) reported by Araoz et al. [[34](#core-collateral-REF34)]. Accordingly, the detection of ventricular septal bowing at pulmonary CTA may be of limited practical value for predicting adverse patient outcome.

### IVC Reflux

The reflux of contrast medium into the IVC represents an indirect sign of increased RV pressure due to various conditions [[35](#core-collateral-REF35)]. It has recently been described as a predictor of mortality in patients with severe PE [[21](#core-collateral-REF21), [36](#core-collateral-REF36), [37](#core-collateral-REF37)]. In our study, substantial IVC reflux was found in 22% and 16% by observers 1 and 2, respectively, which corresponds to the 20% prevalence described by Aviram et al. [[21](#core-collateral-REF21)]. The interobserver variabilities described in their investigation (κ = 0.58–0.78) are comparable to our results (κ = 0.57–0.68). On the other hand, according to Collomb et al. [[20](#core-collateral-REF20)], this sign does not differentiate patients with severe PE from patients with nonsevere PE, although the prevalence of IVC reflux in their study was somewhat smaller (12%).

### RVD/LVD Ratio

Several studies have proposed an increased RVD/LVD ratio as a predictor of short-term mortality after PE [[18](#core-collateral-REF18)–[23](#core-collateral-REF23), [26](#core-collateral-REF26), [34](#core-collateral-REF34), [36](#core-collateral-REF36)–[38](#core-collateral-REF38)], although the prognostic value of this sign remains controversial [[33](#core-collateral-REF33), [34](#core-collateral-REF34)]. Contractor et al. [[18](#core-collateral-REF18)] and Lim et al. [[38](#core-collateral-REF38)] found a RVD/LVD ratio of greater than 1 measured on axial sections indicative of RV strain at pulmonary CTA, whereas others have proposed a threshold of greater than 1.5 [[17](#core-collateral-REF17), [20](#core-collateral-REF20), [26](#core-collateral-REF26)]. However, the axial CT acquisition plane differs from the standard imaging planes of other cardiac imaging techniques, such as echocardiography [[18](#core-collateral-REF18)–[22](#core-collateral-REF22)]. Ventricular measurements on four-chamber views reconstructed from routine pulmonary CTA imaging data were shown to be superior to those from axial views for predicting adverse events. Quiroz et al. [[22](#core-collateral-REF22)] reported that the areas under the curve for predicting adverse events of RVD/LVD ratio measurements based on axial sections and four-chamber views were 0.667 and 0.753, respectively, using an RVD/LVD ratio threshold of greater than 0.9. Schoepf et al. [[23](#core-collateral-REF23)], using the same threshold, found the RVD/LVD ratio on four-chamber views to be predictive of 30-day all-cause mortality with both univariate and multivariate analyses.

Previously, Araoz et al. [[34](#core-collateral-REF34)] reported high interobserver variability for RVD/LVD ratio measurements (intraclass correlation coefficient, 0.51). However, the majority of previous studies reported high agreement for RVD/LVD ratio measurements. Quiroz et al. [[22](#core-collateral-REF22)] reported a Spearman's rank interobserver correlation coefficient of 0.74 for RVD/LVD ratio measurements. Ghuysen et al. [[36](#core-collateral-REF36)] reported similarly high agreement between readers (Spearman's correlation coefficients of *r* = 0.65–0.97). Ghaye et al. [[37](#core-collateral-REF37)] reported Spearman's correlation coefficients ranging from 0.726 to 0.973. In our study, the correlation coefficients between the two observers were highly significant (Spearman's *r* = 0.88 for axial sections and 0.85 for four-chamber views, *p* < 0.001), which is comparable to the prior reports. However, our correlation coefficient (*r* = 0.85) for four-chamber views was slightly lower compared with axial sections (*r* = 0.88). This likely reflects the variability incurred by using workstation manipulations to create four-chamber views with slightly divergent planes chosen by different observers. Conversely, no manipulation of the image plane is involved for evaluating axial sections because the axial plane is fixed and remains constant for different observers.

### RVV/LVV Ratio

We found the strongest interobserver correlation for measurements of RVV/LVV ratio (Spearman's *r* = 0.93). This also reflects the variability incurred by using workstation manipulations to create four-chamber views with slightly divergent planes chosen by different observers. More important, the complex shape of the RV impedes accurate evaluation of this heart chamber on a single image. More precise estimations of RV dimensions could be archived by measuring the ratio of ventricular areas instead of the diameter ratio [[24](#core-collateral-REF24)]. Likely, however, the most suitable method to account for the complex shape of the RV is 3D volumetry because the ventricular boundaries are fairly uniformly and reproducibly demarcated by the endocardial borders and the valvular planes. In a relatively recent study, the RVV/LVV ratios at end-systole and end-diastole were significantly different between patients with and without PE [[27](#core-collateral-REF27)]. Although our study was based on routine, non-ECG-gated pulmonary CTA techniques, interobserver variability for RVV/LVV ratio measurements was very low and lower than for all other CT signs of RV dysfunction investigated here.

### Limitations

The most significant limitation of our study is that we did not correlate the various signs evaluated with outside reference standards, such as echocardiography, and we did not study the prognostic value of our findings for adverse patient outcomes. However, this aspect has been investigated in prior work [[15](#core-collateral-REF15)–[26](#core-collateral-REF26)], and our cohort would be too small to meaningfully contribute to existing data. In this study, we solely aimed at analyzing the observer dependence of establishing the CT signs of RV dysfunction that have hitherto been described in the literature to identify the most robust and reproducible method. Participation of only two observers is another limitation, and more observers would have increased the validity of our findings. Also, for IVC reflux and septal bowing, there might have been better interobserver concordance if standard images rather than simple definitions had been used. Another potential limitation of the current study is that image acquisition by pulmonary CTA was not ECG gated. Non-ECG-gated pulmonary CTA is inevitably inaccurate for measuring ventricular chamber size because the images are acquired in different phases of the cardiac cycle. Although endocardial borders are easily identified on pulmonary CTA, both overestimation and underestimation of the pulmonary CTA-derived RVD/LVD ratio may occur because of motion artifact and insufficient contrast medium attenuation. However, the use of ECG-gated pulmonary CTA protocols over routine non-ECG-gated pulmonary CTA has been shown to result in only limited incremental diagnostic improvements. Because of the additional radiation exposure involved with ECG-gated techniques, this approach is therefore not currently recommended for routine PE imaging [[39](#core-collateral-REF39)]. Last, performance of heart chamber volumetry is somewhat but not substantially more time consuming (mean, 6 minutes 14 seconds for observer 1 and mean, 7 minutes 22 seconds for observer 2) than, for instance, four-chamber view measurements and it would be relatively simple to adapt existing software applications for functional assessment at cardiac CT to nongated pulmonary CTA studies to facilitate automated measurements.

In conclusion, despite these limitations we were able to show that considerable differences exist in the interobserver reproducibility of CT findings of RV dysfunction on pulmonary CTA in patients with acute PE. Cardiac chamber measurements are more reproducible than septal bowing and IVC reflux, which have more limited interobserver agreement for establishing their presence and severity. According to our findings, volumetric determination of the RVV/LVV ratio is the least user dependent and most reproducible. Thus, going forward, we propose the use of volumetric measurements of cardiac chambers to study RV dysfunction in patients with acute PE.
